units.title: Scales and Classification of Map Scales
units.intro: Scale = map distance : ground distance. Three ways: statement (“1 cm to 1 km”), representative fraction (1:100 000), linear bar. Large scale (1:10 000) shows a small area in detail. Small scale (1:1 000 000) shows a big area with little detail.

cards.title: 6.1 Classification of Map Scales
body: Small Scale Maps: This group of map have scales that are smaller than 1:250,000 (like 1:1,000,000).
A city map (like the map of Asmara), land use map of a village, map of a farm, plan map of an airport are all examples of large scale maps.
Represent the farm by a map that is 5 cm long and 5 cm wide.
First, measure the map distance between two consecutive lines of latitude.
**A pantograph** is an instrument used to enlarge or reduce maps.

cards.title: Finding Scale of a Map When it is not given
body: If the printed scale is missing: use a known ground distance between two points. Reducing a map: scale denominator grows (less detail). Enlarging: denominator shrinks.

cards.title: Large scale, large detail
body: Think “large objects on the page.” A town plan is large-scale. A world map is small-scale.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If a map is physically reduced in size, what happens to its scale?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze scale changes during reduction.**
When a map is reduced, its physical dimensions decrease.

**Step 2: Connect to the scale ratio.**
This reduction increases the denominator of the RF, which means the scale becomes smaller.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct option is **The scale becomes smaller.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Two towns are 6 cm apart on a map and 3 km apart on the ground. What is the scale as an RF?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Convert to the same unit: 3 km = 300,000 cm.

**Step 2:** RF = map distance ÷ ground distance = 6 ÷ 300,000 = 1 ÷ 50,000.

**Step 3:** Scale 1:50,000.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 6.3 Map reduction or enlargement
body: Maps often have to be made **smaller (reduced)** or **larger (enlarged)** — for a report, a wall map or to fit a page. When a map is redrawn at a different size, **its scale changes**, so the new scale must be worked out and written on the new map.

**Linear change:** if the length and width are made *k* times as long, the new RF denominator = old denominator ÷ *k*. Example: enlarging a 1:50,000 map **two times** (lengths doubled) gives **1:25,000**; reducing it to **half** the length gives **1:100,000**.

**Area change:** areas change by the square of the linear factor. A map enlarged 2 times in length covers 2² = **4 times** the paper area; reduced to ½ the length it covers ¼ of the area. If a question says the *area* is doubled, the lengths change by √2 ≈ 1.41.

**Methods:** (1) the **square (grid) method** — draw a grid on the original and a grid of larger or smaller squares on the new paper, then copy the detail square by square; (2) the **similar-triangles method**; (3) instruments such as the **pantograph** or a photocopier/computer.
**Remember:** a linear (bar) scale drawn on the map changes size with the map, so it stays correct automatically; an RF or statement scale must be recalculated.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which instrument can be used mechanically to enlarge or reduce maps?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Match instruments with functions.**
- Pantograph: mechanical instrument used to enlarge or reduce drawings/maps.

**Step 2: Confirm alternative instruments.**
Thermometer, barometer, and anemometer are weather instruments.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct instrument is the **Pantograph**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the meaning of '1' in the numerator of a Representative Fraction (RF) scale?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check the properties of an RF scale.**
In an RF scale ($$\frac{1}{\text{Denominator}}$$), the numerator represents map distance.

**Step 2: Identify the correct option.**
The value "1" represents the Map Distance.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct option is **The map distance**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A map with scale 1:50,000 is enlarged two times (linear). What is the new scale?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Enlarging makes map distances bigger, so the RF denominator gets smaller.

**Step 2:** New denominator = 50,000 ÷ 2 = 25,000.

**Step 3:** New scale 1:25,000.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: A drawing of all or part of the earth's surface on a flat surface, reduced to scale.

tips.text: Maps contain certain elements, which guide users to use them properly.
Maps are drawn to scale, because they are drawn on sheets of papers that are much smaller than the area they represent.
Map scale is shown in Word Statement, Representative Fraction or graphic form.
Depending on their scale, maps are classified into small, medium or large scale maps.
Small maps can be enlarged and large maps can be reduced in size.
Enlargement or reduction changes map scale and area.
When instruments are not available, the grid method can be used to enlarge or reduce maps.
Formula: Ground distance = map distance × scale denominator Keep units the same first. 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map = 50 000 cm = 500 m on the ground.
